title: Neural Tube Defects
subject: Paediatrics
summary: Neural tube defects are congenital malformations of the CNS caused by failure of neural tube closure. They present with a spectrum from spina bifida to anencephaly, requiring early diagnosis, multidisciplinary care and prevention with folic acid.

sections.p: Neural tube defects (NTDs) are structural CNS malformations arising from incomplete neural tube closure before 28 days of gestation. Diagnosis is mainly antenatal, but post‑natal signs guide further work‑up.
b: Spina bifida occulta – no visible defect
Spina bifida with meningocele or myelomeningocele – visible sac
Anencephaly – absence of calvarium

t.b: Elevated MSAFP suggests open NTD; normal in occulta
Detects skull vault defects, spinal defects, and associated anomalies
Positive in open NTDs; helps confirm diagnosis when MSAFP is equivocal

sections.p: Severity is graded by the extent of neural tissue involvement and associated anomalies. The Shapiro classification for myelomeningocele is commonly used.
b: Grade I – small meningocele, no neurological deficit
Grade II – myelomeningocele with mild deficit
Grade III – large myelomeningocele, significant deficit

sections.p: NTDs result from a multifactorial interaction of genetics and environment. The most common modifiable risk factor is folate deficiency.
b: Folate deficiency – preventable with 0.4 mg/day before conception and during first trimester
Valproic acid exposure – teratogenic, avoid in women of childbearing age
Maternal diabetes – poorly controlled increases risk
Infections – malaria, HIV, TB can contribute via inflammation

sections.p: Presentation varies with type. Spina bifida may be silent until infancy; anencephaly presents immediately with absent cranial vault. Key signs include visible sac, limb deformities, and neurological deficits.
b: Visible sac or swelling over spine
Weakness or paralysis of lower limbs
Hydrocephalus – bulging fontanelle, vomiting

sections.p: Investigations confirm diagnosis, assess associated anomalies and guide management. In low‑resource settings, focus on clinical exam, basic imaging and serum AFP.

t.b: A normal spine rules out large bony defects
Normal scan reduces likelihood of major NTD
High AFP (>250 µg/L) strongly suggests open defect

sections.p: Early recognition of complications such as hydrocephalus, infection and tethered cord is vital. Red flags include rapid increase in head circumference, vomiting and new neurological deficits.
b: Hydrocephalus – requires shunt
Infection – meningitis, wound infection

sections.p: Management is multidisciplinary: surgical repair, infection prophylaxis, and long‑term neuro‑rehabilitation. Folic acid supplementation is essential for prevention.
b: Surgical closure within 24–48 hrs of birth for myelomeningocele

t.b: Avoid broad‑spectrum agents to reduce resistance
Reduces recurrence risk in future pregnancies

sections.p: Regular neuro‑developmental assessment, bladder and bowel management, and early intervention services are key. Prevention hinges on periconceptional folic acid and avoidance of teratogens.
b: Annual neuro‑psychological testing

sections.p: Spina bifida occulta may be mistaken for simple back pain; meningitis can mimic early hydrocephalus signs.
b: Spina bifida occulta – no visible sac, often asymptomatic

sections.p: Serum AFP can be falsely normal in late‑presenting open NTDs or in occulta. Ultrasound may miss small defects if performed after 20 weeks.
Urgent referral if signs of increased intracranial pressure, wound infection, or new neurological deficits develop.
b: Bulging fontanelle
Rapidly increasing head circumference
Severe vomiting
New weakness or paralysis

faq.q: Why is folic acid so important for NTD prevention?
faq.a: Folate is essential for DNA synthesis and cell division; deficiency disrupts neural tube closure.

faq.q: Can an infant with anencephaly survive?
faq.a: No; anencephaly is incompatible with life beyond a few hours to days.

faq.q: What is the most common teratogenic drug causing NTDs?
faq.a: Valproic acid is the most widely recognized teratogen linked to NTDs.

exam: A 28‑day‑old infant presents with a visible sac over the lumbar spine. What is the next best step? — Immediate surgical referral for myelomeningocele repair and prophylactic antibiotics.
A mother on valproic acid reports a pregnancy. What advice should you give? — Discontinue valproic acid, start high‑dose folic acid 5 mg/day, and refer for early anomaly scan.
A child with spina bifida has a sudden increase in head circumference. What is the likely complication? — Hydrocephalus; urgent neuro‑imaging and neurosurgical evaluation.
A 2‑year‑old with spina bifida develops urinary urgency. What is the most likely cause? — Neurogenic bladder; refer to urology for clean intermittent catheterisation.
A newborn with a small sac over the spine has normal neuro exam. What is the likely diagnosis? — Spina bifida occulta; no immediate surgery needed.
A mother with poorly controlled diabetes has a baby with a neural tube defect. What is the main preventive measure? — Tight glycaemic control before conception and during pregnancy.
